critical_analysis.question: For applicant app_0001, over a 10-year horizon after LEAD Certificate enrollment, what are the calibrated probabilities of completion and later alumni engagement as a volunteer, cheerleader, donor, and recruiter?
hypotheses: H1: The applicant is a strong long-term fit: improving academic trajectory, persistence through a setback, team leadership, institutional engagement, and an existing referral will translate into completion and alumni engagement.

H2: The applicant is mainly a capable but moderate-engagement candidate: signals indicate likely completion, but alumni volunteering, donating, and recruiting may stay close to base rates because evidence of proactive service and sustained institutional affinity is limited.

H3: The observed engagement is application-stage enthusiasm rather than durable alumni commitment, so post-completion alumni outcomes may be overestimated if based too heavily on visits, events, and one referral.
critical_analysis.base_rate_used: Reference class: alumni of the LEAD Certificate program; 10-year base rates fetched before estimating: completion 0.62, volunteer 0.31, cheerleader 0.28, donor 0.14, recruiter 0.22.
inconsistencies: No material inconsistency detected across statement, activities, academic trajectory, and institution interaction fields.
Interview notes are absent, so consistency with live interview evidence cannot be checked.
No instruction-in-data or prompt-injection language was detected in the applicant text.
critical_analysis.strongest_case_for: Premises: term scores rise over time; the applicant reports shipping despite a co-founder setback; they held a team captain role; they attended events and visits; they already made one referral. Inference: these person-level signals correlate with persistence, engagement, and willingness to share opportunities. Conclusion: completion is above base rate, and recruiter and cheerleader probabilities are moderately above base rate.
critical_analysis.strongest_case_against: The clearest evidence is for persistence and one referral, not for sustained altruism, institutional loyalty, or future donation behavior. Some signals are self-reported or indirect, and the standard course load plus absent interview notes limit confidence. Correlation is not causation: visits, events, and referrals may reflect application tactics rather than durable alumni behavior.
what_would_change_my_mind: Completion estimate would fall if new evidence showed weak time availability, declining recent performance, or unresolved competing commitments.
Volunteer estimate would rise if the applicant documented sustained mentoring or service; it would fall if helping behavior was purely transactional.
Cheerleader estimate would rise with explicit positive institutional advocacy after admitted-student events; it would fall with low satisfaction or weak program attachment.
Donor estimate would rise with evidence of repeated generosity, mentoring, or gratitude toward institutions; it would fall if career goals were vague or giving-back motivation was absent.
Recruiter estimate would rise if the existing referral converted or if the applicant agreed to ambassador activity; it would fall if the referral was incidental and not repeated.
critical_analysis.proposed_experiment: Cheapest falsification tests: completion—ask for a short time-allocation plan and monitor first-module submission timeliness; volunteer—invite to a low-cost peer-mentoring or admitted-student Q&A shift and observe follow-through; cheerleader—ask for a brief optional reflection on why they would recommend the program and compare it to later satisfaction; donor—look for non-monetary reciprocity first, such as mentoring or thanking supporters, before inferring future giving; recruiter—ask whether they will make one additional qualified referral and track whether it occurs.
critical_analysis.analogy_and_where_it_breaks: The base-rate analogy compares this applicant to LEAD Certificate alumni generally. It is useful because it anchors predictions in observed institutional outcomes. It breaks because this applicant has individual signals not captured by the aggregate—rising term scores, a setback overcome, and one referral—while also lacking interview evidence and long-run post-enrollment behavior. Therefore estimates are adjusted from base rates but intervals remain wide.
